tagline: Four miles of island road, with a ferry crossing from Edgartown
intro: Chappaquiddick Road covers four miles on the island off Martha’s Vineyard’s eastern end. MassDOT’s scenic-byways map describes it winding along the island’s coast to the point, offering views of the smaller Vineyard islands. Chappaquiddick and Poucha roads are paved, with sandy woodland roads and trails branching toward shorelines. Red cedar woods, salt marshes and salty ponds are part of the island landscape.

The ferry connection has its own history: the original On Time was built in less than two weeks for Foster B. Silva’s takeover of the service on August 1, 1948. Captain Samuel B. Norton and boatbuilder Manuel Swartz Roberts led the crew that launched it on time. Its ferry service ended in 1975, after which it became a freshwater barge for visiting yachts. The island’s land connection is less fixed: Norton Point is a narrow barrier beach joining it to Martha’s Vineyard, and hurricanes and strong storms can breach that link for periods of time.

The approach begins in Edgartown, where ferries carry pedestrians, bicycles and up to three cars at a time to Chappaquiddick. Across the island, Mytoi places a Japanese garden in pine forest. Cape Poge Light stands at the northeast tip, a separate excursion beyond the paved-road journey.

moments.title: Edgartown
moments.text: Water Street’s captains’ houses belong to Edgartown’s years as a whaling port. Whaling dominated the town’s economy during its nineteenth-century heyday, and Greek Revival architecture accounts for much of the village’s building stock. Many houses from that period are one-and-a-half-story cottages with modest details such as corner pilasters. The historic district includes elaborate ship captains’ houses alongside the courthouse, Federated Church and Whaling Church. As whaling and the village economy declined, comparatively few Victorian buildings followed. Later summer houses, built between 1895 and about 1930, predominantly used Colonial Revival styling.

moments.title: Mytoi
moments.text: An arched footbridge leads to an island in Mytoi’s small pond. This Japanese garden occupies an open pine forest on Chappaquiddick. Mary Wakeman gave the property to The Trustees of Reservations in 1976. The organization extended it in 1981 and owns and maintains the garden.
moments.notice: An arched footbridge crosses to the island in the garden’s pond.

moments.title: Cape Poge Light
moments.text: Cape Poge’s white wooden tower dates to 1893, but the light station began in 1801. During the War of 1812, the first light was extinguished for a few months, and its apparatus was hidden in a Chappaquiddick house’s cellar. The first lighthouse moved twice as its bluff eroded, and replacement towers followed in 1844 and 1880. The current tower has moved four times, most recently by helicopter in 1987. It is a 35-foot conical structure at Chappaquiddick’s northeast tip. The light was automated in 1943; its solar-powered beacon now flashes white every six seconds.
